title: Counting and Comparing Collections to 20
seo_title: Foundation Counting and Comparing Worksheets: More, Fewer, the Same to 20 (Free, with Answers)
standard_text: Quantify and compare collections to at least 20 using counting and explain or demonstrate reasoning.
meta_desc: Free Foundation (Prep, Kindergarten) maths worksheets on counting and comparing collections to 20, matched to the Australian Curriculum (AC9MFN03): count on past 10, match one to one, more, fewer, the same, most and fewest. 100 picture questions with answers.
key_big: Match one to one: the group with some left over has more.
key_sub: Count each thing once. A longer row is not always more. Say how you know.
body_html:
Count to 20

Touch each thing once. When there are more than 10, count the first 10, then count on: 11, 12, 13 …

Match one to one

Line up two groups. The group with things left over has more. The other has fewer. If nothing is left over, they are the same.

Explain your thinking

Say why: 15 comes after 12 when we count, so 15 is more.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do
Thinking a longer row has moreMatch or count both rows
Mixing up more and fewerMore has some left over
Answering 7 for 'how many more' when there are 7 and 5Count only the ones left over: 2

faq.q: What does quantify and compare collections mean?
faq.a: It means counting how many are in a group and saying which group has more, fewer or the same. Foundation students do this for collections up to at least 20 (AC9MFN03).

faq.q: Why does my child think a spread-out row has more?
faq.a: Young children often judge by length. Match the two rows one to one or count both to show the number stays the same.

faq.q: How can my child explain which group has more?
faq.a: Encourage sentences like: There are 2 left over, so there are more apples, or 15 comes after 12 when we count, so 15 is more.

faq.q: What can we count at home?
faq.a: Count pegs, shells, socks or toy cars up to 20, then compare two piles. Ask: Which has more? How do you know?

items.q: Are there more apples or more cups?
items.e: Match them one to one. Some apples have no partner, so there are more apples. More apples.
